newsitem.title: UK: Low-status work can cause heart disease - study.
newsitem.headline: Low-status work can cause heart disease - study.

text.p: British researchers on Friday confirmed that low job status and having little control over work life can cause heart disease.

The final instalment of a series of reports known as Whitehall studies -- named after the London street where many government departments are located -- shows it is not the top executives who die of heart attacks, but their clerks and secretaries.

Epidemiologist Michael Marmot of University College London and colleagues surveyed 7,300 civil servants three times between 1985 and 1993. They also checked any signs of heart disease, such as chest pain.
Men and women in clerical and office-support grades were more likely to develop heart disease than those in administrator grades, they found.
In the third study they took careful care to account for smoking -- people of lower social status smoke more -- and poor nutrition.
Even with this taken into account, the lower the grade and the less the control, the more likely people were to suffer from heart disease.

"Our findings build on evidence that psychosocial factors are important in the aetiology of CHD (coronary heart disease), since they suggest that such factors have an important role in the generation of social inequalities in CHD," Marmot's group wrote in their report in the Lancet medical journal.
"Greater attention to the design of work environments may be one important way to reduce inequalities in health."
Other experts agreed that it was a lot easier to give people a little more control at work than to try to change their social status.

"If these findings are replicated by others, they are of great importance because they shed light not only on employment-grade inequality in health but also on social-class inequalities in the general population," Leonard Syme and Jennifer Balfour of the University of California at Berkeley said in a commentary.
"Although it may be difficult to intervene on social class inequalities in health, there are more opportunities to intervene on control," they added.
"It may also be possible to change environmental forces, in the workplace or the community so that more flexibility and control is available."
